passage: From the window of my flat I can see the nursery school's courtyard, and every morning I watch Aadhya, five, walk in and go straight to the bench where Ira waits. Aadhya sits so close their sleeves touch, and swings her legs in time with Ira's. Today, though, after a quarrel over the red bucket, Aadhya sat at the far end of the bench, looking at the sand. By lunch she had shuffled back next to Ira. I can't say what they said to each other.

qa.q: Where does Aadhya go every morning?
qa.a: She goes straight to the bench where Ira waits.

qa.q: What might Aadhya's choice of seats say about how she felt today?
qa.a: Sitting at the far end after the quarrel suggests she was upset with Ira, and shuffling back by lunch suggests the quarrel had eased. Kids also move seats for fun, so it's only a guess.

qa.q: What could an adult watching do if a child keeps sitting apart from a friend?
qa.a: They can watch the pattern over several days before deciding anything, and stay ready to help if the child seems upset.

qa.q: How might Ira feel when Aadhya sits at the far end?
qa.a: Ira may feel unsure or a little hurt, and glad when Aadhya returns to sit close again.

grounding: Sitting close shows liking and comfort, while shifting away can show a quarrel, seen by an observer who can only guess.

passage:
Day one: at the Bristol nursery, Jyoti, five, walked into the reading corner and sat down right next to Rehana. Their knees touched as they looked at the same book.
Day three: Jyoti chose the beanbag across the room and pulled out a puzzle. Rehana didn't say anything but went to the shelf by herself.
Day five: after a shared snack, Jyoti dragged her cushion beside Rehana again and whispered, "Can I see your page?" Rehana shifted over to make space.

qa.q: What did Jyoti do on day five to sit next to Rehana?
qa.a: She dragged her cushion beside Rehana.

qa.q: What might Jyoti's move to the beanbag on day three suggest, and what does the pattern of days add?
qa.a: The move might mean a quarrel or a wish to be apart, but she chose the puzzle, so it might just have been for fun. Coming back to sit close on day five suggests she still likes Rehana.

qa.q: What could the teacher do if a child keeps changing seats?
qa.a: The teacher can watch the pattern over several days, and check in gently if a child seems left out or upset.

qa.q: How might Rehana feel when Jyoti sits beside her again?
qa.a: She may feel pleased and reassured, since she moved over to make space.

grounding: Choosing a seat beside a friend shows liking and comfort, and patterns across days matter more than one moment.
